summary: Teredo lets nodes behind one or more IPv4 NATs obtain IPv6 connectivity by tunneling IPv6 packets over UDP. It relies on Teredo servers and relays; the servers are stateless and handle only a small fraction of the traffic. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: If you are stuck behind a door that only speaks the old language, Teredo wraps new-language messages in old-language envelopes so they can pass through.

questions: how to get ipv6 behind a nat
does teredo work behind symmetric nat
subtitle: How a host behind an IPv4 NAT can reach the IPv6 Internet by wrapping IPv6 packets in UDP.

tldr.problem: Hosts behind IPv4 NATs cannot use ordinary IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling, because NATs are typically not programmed to pass arbitrary payload types, and 6to4 needs the 6to4 router to be in the NAT box.
tldr.mechanism: Teredo sends IPv6 packets as UDP payload. A client learns its public IPv4 address and port from a stateless Teredo server, builds an IPv6 address that embeds them, and exchanges small packets called bubbles to open NAT mappings. Teredo relays connect it to the native IPv6 Internet.
tldr.outcome: The RFC presents Teredo as an interim, last-resort mechanism with a built-in exit: once a host gets IPv6 by other means it should stop using Teredo. It is updated by RFC 5991, RFC 6081 and RFC 9601.

today: RFC 4380 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 5991, RFC 6081 and RFC 9601. The RFC itself describes Teredo as an interim, last-resort transition mechanism that clients, servers and relays are expected to retire.

sections.title: The Problem Teredo Solves
sections.content:
Classic IPv6 transition tunnels send IPv6 packets as the payload of IPv4 packets, and 6to4 (RFC 3056) adds automatic discovery. These methods fail for a host isolated behind a NAT (Network Address Translator): NATs are typically not programmed to pass arbitrary payload types, and the host's local address cannot be used in a 6to4 scheme. 6to4 works only when the NAT and the 6to4 router are in the same box.

Tunnel brokers are another option, but traffic takes a dogleg route and the broker must carry all of it. Teredo instead aims for automatic tunneling along a direct path. Because TCP and UDP are the only protocols guaranteed to cross most NATs, and tunneling over TCP would give poor quality of service, Teredo carries IPv6 as the payload of UDP.

The service is built from four kinds of node: Teredo clients (hosts that want IPv6), Teredo servers (helpers with a globally routable IPv4 address), Teredo relays (IPv6 routers that forward traffic between the Teredo service and native IPv6) and plain IPv6 nodes. Servers listen on UDP port 3544.
sections.eli5: Some home routers will not let new-style internet messages through. Teredo hides them inside a kind of message the router already knows how to pass.

sections.title: Design Goals and Model of Operation
sections.content:
Teredo assumes how NATs treat UDP. It works behind cone, restricted cone and port-restricted cone NATs, as classified in RFC 3489. Behind a symmetric NAT it works only if the user can reserve a fixed UDP port for each client, for example with the NAT's DMZ function. Because NAT mappings expire, clients must send keep-alive traffic; the default refresh interval is 30 seconds.

The design aims to be an "IPv6 provider of last resort". Hosts SHOULD prefer direct IPv6, a 6to4 router co-located with the NAT, or a configured tunnel, and SHOULD prefer 6to4 if they have a global IPv4 address. Servers are meant to be stateless and to avoid carrying data traffic, so they can be replicated and scaled; data flows directly between clients, or through a relay for native IPv6 peers.

A client first runs a qualification procedure against a server. To reach a native IPv6 or 6to4 peer, it sends an ICMP echo request (carrying a large random number) via its server; the reply is routed to the relay nearest the peer, and the client learns that relay's IPv4 address and UDP port. The server only takes part in qualification and in exchanging bubbles and ICMP echo requests, which limits load and privacy exposure.
sections.eli5: A helper server tells you what your address looks like from the outside. After that, you mostly talk straight to your friends, and the helper only gets involved to introduce you.

sections.title: Teredo Addresses
sections.content:
A Teredo IPv6 address has five parts: the 32-bit Teredo service prefix, the server's IPv4 address, 16 flag bits, the client's UDP port and the client's IPv4 address. The global service prefix is 2001:0000::/32.

The port and IPv4 address are the client's mapped (post-NAT) values, and both are obfuscated by flipping every bit (XOR with 0xFFFF and 0xFFFFFFFF). This keeps NATs that rewrite embedded 32-bit values from corrupting them.

In the flags, the top bit C is the cone bit: 1 if the client believes it is behind a cone NAT, 0 otherwise. The UG bits are 00 and the other bits are zero. So the only specified flag values are 0x0000 and 0x8000.

Because the address embeds an IPv4 address and port, it stays valid only as long as that mapping does.
sections.eli5: A Teredo address is like a street address that has the front-door number of your outside mailbox written into it, just scrambled a bit.

sections.title: Encapsulation and MTU
sections.content:
Teredo packets are UDP datagrams inside IPv4. With simple encapsulation the UDP payload is just the IPv6 packet. A server relaying a packet from a third party may add an origin indication: an 8-octet element (two null octets, the obfuscated port, the obfuscated IPv4 address) that tells a client where the packet came from.

Router Solicitation and Router Advertisement exchanges may carry an authentication element that starts with octets 0x00 0x01, then an ID length, an authentication-value length, the client identifier, the value, an 8-octet nonce and a confirmation byte. The default algorithm uses HMAC (RFC 2104) with SHA1. If both lengths are null, only the nonce is checked.

The default link MTU, and the one a server supplies, SHOULD be the IPv6 minimum of 1280 bytes. Implementations SHOULD NOT set the Don't Fragment bit on the IPv4 header.
sections.eli5: Each packet is a letter in an envelope. Sometimes the helper adds a sticky note saying where the letter really came from, and sometimes a secret code to prove the helper is who it claims to be.

sections.title: Client Qualification and Bubbles
sections.content:
To qualify, a client in the "initial" state sends a Router Solicitation over UDP to the server's Teredo port with the cone bit set to 1, and waits for a Router Advertisement. The defaults are a 4-second timeout and 3 repetitions. With no answer, it clears the cone bit and tries again; if that also fails, it goes "off-line". A valid reply carries an origin indication, from which the client learns its mapped address and port.

If the reply came with the cone bit set, the client is behind a cone NAT. If not, the client repeats the exchange with the server's secondary IPv4 address. A different mapped address or port means a symmetric NAT and Teredo cannot be used. The same values mean a (port-)restricted cone NAT, and the client is qualified.

To talk to a peer behind a non-cone NAT, clients exchange bubbles, minimal IPv6 packets with no payload (next header 59), to create NAT mappings. A direct bubble goes to the peer's mapped address; an indirect bubble goes through the peer's server. A client MUST NOT send a bubble less than 2 seconds after its last one to that peer, nor after 4 bubbles in 300 seconds with no direct response.

Clients keep a list of recent peers, mark each as trusted or not, and refresh the server mapping when no packet has arrived within a randomized refresh interval (75 to 100 percent of the refresh interval).
sections.eli5: First the client asks the helper, "what do I look like from outside?" Then, to reach a friend, it throws a tiny empty ball at the friend's door so the friend's door lets the reply back in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC groups the risks into four kinds: exposing a host directly to the IPv6 Internet, man-in-the-middle attacks by spoofing a server, denial of service against Teredo clients, and denial of service against non-Teredo nodes.

On exposure, a Teredo host gives up whatever firewall service its NAT offered, so its listening services become targets for the whole IPv6 Internet. The RFC lists three mitigations: restrict some services to link-local addresses (which Teredo does not carry), run a local firewall (recommended), and use IPsec where keys can be negotiated.

To resist a spoofed Router Advertisement, the simple nonce check defeats any attacker who is not on path, and secure qualification with a shared secret adds further protection; the secret should contain sufficient entropy. Hosts should be generous in what they accept and careful in what they send, so a client verifies a new peer address with an ICMPv6 echo carrying a random nonce, recommended to be at least 64 bits long.
sections.eli5: Opening a door to the whole internet is risky, so Teredo tells you to keep your own lock on the door and to double-check that anyone claiming to be a helper is the real one.

sections.title: Interim by Design: IAB Considerations
sections.content:
Section 8 answers the IAB's requirements for "Unilateral Self Address Fixing" (UNSAF) mechanisms (RFC 3424). It states the narrow problem, an exit strategy and the system's brittleness.

The built-in exit: as soon as a client gets IPv6 through 6to4 or native service, it can stop using Teredo. The RFC expects home routers to become IPv6 routers, and expects relay operators to turn relays off as traffic falls. Teredo servers are expected to announce a date when they will stop, and most are not expected to run more than a few years. Nodes MUST NOT act as Teredo clients if they already have IPv6 by another means.

The brittleness it admits: reliance on a classification of NAT behavior, the need to keep refreshing mappings, a server and relays as extra points of failure, no support behind symmetric NATs, and jitter from queuing packets while bubbles are exchanged, which can hurt latency-sensitive uses such as VoIP. Its long-term requirement is that devices doing IPv4 NAT should also become IPv6 routers.
sections.eli5: Teredo calls itself a temporary bridge. Once the road is built, everyone is supposed to stop using the bridge.
